title: Mannheim water capacity constraint and development impacts
subtitle: Also: Fischer Hallman expropriation, street design guidelines, integrated mobility plan, school-zone road safety after speed camera cancellation.
overview: Most of the day went to the Mannheim service area water capacity constraint, which serves Kitchener, Waterloo and parts of Cambridge, Woolwich and Wilmot. Staff said a revised method for measuring capacity, including a 20% operational resiliency buffer, shows the system cannot support new development approvals or new servicing agreements for now. Existing building permits have not been withdrawn. Ten delegations, mostly from the development industry, asked for clarity, consistent messaging and an industry task force.

The committee recommended that staff make a preliminary list of short, medium and long-term repair plans public before the end of January {{vote:m7}}. It also recommended that staff report on water conservation policy options by June {{vote:m9}} and share the underlying data with area municipalities {{vote:m10}}. Staff will report in February on which developments and applications receive regional advisory comments {{vote:m14}}. Proposals for a detailed information package and for finding unused capacity were defeated.

The committee also recommended starting expropriation of temporary easements for Fischer Hallman Road work {{vote:m6}} and received the Integrated Mobility Plan outline for information. A road safety motion on school zones was deferred to the January 28 Council meeting. All recommendations go to Council.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that staff publish a preliminary list of short, medium and long-term infrastructure repair plans before the end of January 2026, instead of late in the first quarter, with Council receiving it at least 48 hours before the public {{vote:m7}}.

The committee recommended that staff give area municipalities the raw data behind the Agile Water Supply Peer Review by the end of January and report to Council by January 28 on sharing it with industry and community partners, along with planned infrastructure works, capacity gains and timing.

The committee recommended that staff report by the end of June 2026 with water conservation policy options, seeking input from community partners, the development sector, the Grand River Conservation Authority and area municipalities.
The committee recommended that staff report to its February 2026 meeting on which types of developments and applications are subject to Regional advisory comments.

The committee recommended authorizing the Regional Solicitor to begin expropriating six temporary grading easements for Fischer Hallman Road improvements between Bleams Road and Plains Road in Kitchener.

debate: Delegates from the development industry said uncertainty was the main problem. They said lenders and investors were pulling back, skilled trades could leave the region, and planners were giving inconsistent answers about what could proceed. Several asked for an industry task force and for a phased-in resiliency buffer.

Staff said the 20% buffer is the minimum needed to take equipment offline for repairs and cover failures, and that the system already shows stress. A consultant presented charts showing that much of that buffer is already used up by current outages. Staff said phasing it in would not work.

Some councillors asked whether the shift from earlier assurances of ample capacity was explained well enough. Others questioned how the issue was communicated to media. Staff said the technical complexity led them to hold detailed one-on-one briefings.

On the preliminary repair list, staff warned it would be unvetted and incomplete, with no costs or firm timelines yet. Some councillors preferred waiting until the end of February, but a proposal to move the date was defeated. Others said speed mattered more.

A broader information package was defeated. Councillors called it too prescriptive and said it overloaded staff who are already stretched. A proposal to find unused capacity was also defeated. Councillors worried it would pit developers and municipalities against each other while the system is in deficit.
